patches.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1169738147207">The second law of thermodynamics deals with the direction taken by spontaneous processes. Many processes occur spontaneously in one direction only—that is, they are irreversible, under a given set of conditions. Here are some examples of irreversible processes seen in day-to-day life: a glass breaking, heat transferring from a hot object to a cold object, conversion of kinetic energy into thermal energy, and a puff of gas expanding from a corner of a vacuum chamber into the entire chamber. If you saw a video of glass un-breaking, or two objects in thermal contact where one gets hotter and the other gets colder, or a hot stationary object spontaneously cooling off and moving in some direction, or a gas in a chamber "regrouping" into a corner, you would say this is a video run backwards. This is because you intuitively recognize these are examples of <term id="import-auto-id1169737952026">irreversible process</term>, and these processes in nature only take place in the forward direction, not reverse (See <link target-id="import-auto-id1169737796666" />).</para>
patches.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1169738147207">The second law of thermodynamics deals with the direction taken by spontaneous processes. Many processes occur spontaneously in one direction only—that is, they are irreversible, under a given set of conditions. Here are some examples of irreversible processes seen in day-to-day life: a glass breaking, heat transferring from a hot object to a cold object, conversion of kinetic energy into thermal energy, and a puff of gas expanding from a corner of a vacuum chamber into the entire chamber. If you saw a video of glass un-breaking, or two objects in thermal contact where the hotter one gets hotter and the colder one gets colder, or a hot stationary object spontaneously cooling off and moving in some direction, or a gas in a chamber "regrouping" into a corner, you would say this is a video run backwards. This is because you intuitively recognize these are examples of <term id="import-auto-id1169737952026">irreversible process</term>, and these processes in nature only take place in the forward direction, not reverse (See <link target-id="import-auto-id1169737796666" />).</para>

patches.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="eip-id1423437">It is impossible in any system for heat transfer from a reservoir to completely convert to work in a cyclical process in which the system returns to its initial state.</para>
patches.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="eip-id1423437">It is impossible for a system operating in a cycle to have as its sole result the absorption of heat from a single reservoir and the conversion of all that heat into work.</para>

patches.before_xml: <item xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1169738234744">The two expressions of the second law of thermodynamics are: (i) Heat transfer occurs spontaneously from higher- to lower-temperature bodies but never spontaneously in the reverse direction; and (ii) It is impossible in any system for heat transfer from a reservoir to completely convert to work in a cyclical process in which the system returns to its initial state. These expressions describe the direction of irreversible processes that occur in nature.</item>
patches.proposed_xml: <item xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1169738234744">The two expressions of the second law of thermodynamics are: (i) Heat transfer occurs spontaneously from higher- to lower-temperature bodies but never spontaneously in the reverse direction; and (ii) It is impossible for a system operating in a cycle to have as its sole result the absorption of heat from a single reservoir and the conversion of all that heat into work. These expressions describe the direction of irreversible processes that occur in nature.</item>

patches.before_xml: <meaning xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="fs-id1169738014671">heat transfer flows from a hotter to a cooler object, never the reverse, and some heat energy in any process is lost to available work in a cyclical process</meaning>
patches.proposed_xml: <meaning xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="fs-id1169738014671">heat does not spontaneously flow from a cooler to a hotter object, and no cyclic engine can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work as its sole result</meaning>

patches.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="eip-567">If all the work output is converted to electricity in a period of one day, the average power output is 1180 MW (this is left to you as an end-of-chapter problem). This value is about the size of a large-scale conventional power plant. The efficiency found is acceptably close to the value of 42% given for coal power stations. It means that fully 59.2% of the energy is heat transfer to the environment, which usually results in warming lakes, rivers, or the ocean near the power station, and is implicated in a warming planet generally. While the laws of thermodynamics limit the efficiency of such plants—including plants fired by nuclear fuel, oil, and natural gas—the heat transfer to the environment could be, and sometimes is, used for heating homes or for industrial processes. The generally low cost of energy has not made it economical to make better use of the waste heat transfer from most heat engines. Coal-fired power plants produce the greatest amount of <sub><m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mtext>CO</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>2</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"CO" rSub { size 8{2} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math></sub> per unit energy output (compared to natural gas or oil), making coal the least efficient fossil fuel.</para>
patches.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="eip-567">If all the work output is converted to electricity in a period of one day, the average power output is 1180 MW (this is left to you as an end-of-chapter problem). This value is about the size of a large-scale conventional power plant. The efficiency is 40.8%, so 59.2% of the heat input is transferred to the environment. This can warm nearby bodies of water used for cooling. While the laws of thermodynamics limit the efficiency of such plants—including plants fired by nuclear fuel, oil, and natural gas—the heat transfer to the environment could be, and sometimes is, used for heating homes or for industrial processes. Coal combustion also releases <m:math><m:msub><m:mtext>CO</m:mtext><m:mn>2</m:mn></m:msub></m:math>, which contributes to global warming. Coal generally produces more <m:math><m:msub><m:mtext>CO</m:mtext><m:mn>2</m:mn></m:msub></m:math> per unit of heat released than oil or natural gas.</para>

patches.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1169736614771">With the information given in <link target-id="fs-id1169737966074" />, we can find characteristics such as the efficiency of a heat engine without any knowledge of how the heat engine operates, but looking further into the mechanism of the engine will give us greater insight. <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738202073" /> illustrates the operation of the common four-stroke gasoline engine. The four steps shown complete this heat engine’s cycle, bringing the gasoline-air mixture back to its original condition.</para>
patches.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1169736614771">With the information given in <link target-id="fs-id1169737966074" />, we can find characteristics such as the efficiency of a heat engine without any knowledge of how the heat engine operates, but looking further into the mechanism of the engine will give us greater insight. <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738202073" /> illustrates the operation of the common four-stroke gasoline engine. The four steps shown complete the engine’s operating cycle, replacing the exhaust gases with a fresh gasoline-air mixture.</para>

patches.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1169737933345">The <term id="import-auto-id1169737845754">Otto cycle</term> shown in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738036935" />(a) is used in four-stroke internal combustion engines, although in fact the true Otto cycle paths do not correspond exactly to the strokes of the engine.</para>
patches.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1169737933345">The ideal <term id="import-auto-id1169737845754">Otto cycle</term> shown in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738036935" /> models a fixed amount of gas undergoing two adiabatic and two constant-volume processes. It approximates the operation of a four-stroke internal combustion engine, although its paths do not correspond exactly to the strokes of the engine.</para>

patches.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1169738110852">The adiabatic process AB corresponds to the nearly adiabatic compression stroke of the gasoline engine. In both cases, work is done on the system (the gas mixture in the cylinder), increasing its temperature and pressure. Along path BC of the Otto cycle, heat transfer <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>h</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{h} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> into the gas occurs at constant volume, causing a further increase in pressure and temperature. This process corresponds to burning fuel in an internal combustion engine, and takes place so rapidly that the volume is nearly constant. Path CD in the Otto cycle is an adiabatic expansion that does work on the outside world, just as the power stroke of an internal combustion engine does in its nearly adiabatic expansion. The work done by the system along path CD is greater than the work done on the system along path AB, because the pressure is greater, and so there is a net work output. Along path DA in the Otto cycle, heat transfer <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{c} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> from the gas at constant volume reduces its temperature and pressure, returning it to its original state. In an internal combustion engine, this process corresponds to the exhaust of hot gases and the intake of an air-gasoline mixture at a considerably lower temperature. In both cases, heat transfer into the environment occurs along this final path.</para>
patches.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1169738110852">The adiabatic process AB corresponds to the nearly adiabatic compression stroke of the gasoline engine. In both cases, work is done on the system (the gas mixture in the cylinder), increasing its temperature and pressure. Along path BC of the Otto cycle, heat transfer <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>h</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{h} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> into the gas occurs at constant volume, causing a further increase in pressure and temperature. This process corresponds to burning fuel in an internal combustion engine, and takes place so rapidly that the volume is nearly constant. Path CD in the Otto cycle is an adiabatic expansion that does work on the outside world, just as the power stroke of an internal combustion engine does in its nearly adiabatic expansion. The work done by the system along path CD is greater than the work done on the system along path AB, because the pressure is greater, and so there is a net work output. Along path DA in the Otto cycle, heat transfer <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{c} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> from the gas at constant volume reduces its temperature and pressure, returning it to its original state. In an internal combustion engine, this part of the model represents the exhaust of hot gases and the intake of a cooler air-gasoline mixture. The actual engine carries energy out with the exhaust; the ideal cycle represents this by heat transfer from the gas.</para>

patches.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1169736654385">The net work done by a cyclical process is the area inside the closed path on a <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mstyle fontstyle="italic"><m:mrow><m:mtext>PV</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mstyle></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ ital "PV"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> diagram, such as that inside path ABCDA in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738036935" />. Note that in every imaginable cyclical process, it is absolutely necessary for heat transfer from the system to occur in order to get a net work output. In the Otto cycle, heat transfer occurs along path DA. If no heat transfer occurs, then the return path is the same, and the net work output is zero. The lower the temperature on the path AB, the less work has to be done to compress the gas. The area inside the closed path is then greater, and so the engine does more work and is thus more efficient. Similarly, the higher the temperature along path CD, the more work output there is. (See <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738093819" />.) So efficiency is related to the temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs. In the next section, we shall see what the absolute limit to the efficiency of a heat engine is, and how it is related to temperature.</para>
patches.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1169736654385">The net work done by a cyclical process is the area inside the closed path on a PV diagram, such as that inside path ABCDA in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738036935" />. A heat-engine cycle must reject some of its heat input. In the Otto cycle, this heat transfer occurs along path DA. Simply retracing the reversible adiabatic expansion would give no net work output. Lower pressure along AB reduces the compression work, while higher pressure along CD increases the expansion work. These changes increase the net work output of the Otto cycle. The maximum possible efficiency of a heat engine operating between two heat reservoirs increases when the hot reservoir is hotter or the cold reservoir is colder. In the next section, we shall see how these reservoir temperatures set the upper limit to efficiency.</para>
